title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Brontë
openingText: There was no possibility of taking a walk that day. We had been wandering, indeed, in the leafless shrubbery an hour in the morning; but since dinner (Mrs. Reed, when there was no company, dined early) the cold winter wind had brought with it clouds so sombre, and a rain so penetrating, that further out-door exercise was now out of the question.
about:
Jane Eyre is the autobiographical novel of an orphan girl, raised by an unloving aunt, sent to a brutal charity school, and finally hired as a governess at Thornfield Hall — where she meets Mr. Rochester, the master of the house, and his secrets. The novel is told in the first person, in Jane's voice — small, ironic, fierce — and follows her from age ten to her marriage.

Charlotte Brontë published it in 1847 under the pseudonym Currer Bell. It was an immediate success and remains one of the most read English novels. Its first-person voice — a poor, plain, intelligent woman insisting on her own moral worth — was new in 1847 and is still uncommon.

angleCards.title: Jane's refusal to be diminished.
angleCards.text: Every man in this novel tries to define Jane on his own terms — Brocklehurst as sinner, Rochester as possession, St. John as instrument. I want to track how she resists each of them and what it costs her.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Jane Eyre to follow Jane's refusal to be diminished — by class, by Rochester, by St. John — and to understand what it costs her and what she refuses to surrender even for love.

angleCards.title: The madwoman in the attic.
angleCards.text: Bertha Mason is the wife locked in the third floor — passionate, colonial, inconvenient. I want to read the novel asking what she represents and whose story is really being told.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Jane Eyre with Bertha Mason in mind — the madwoman in the attic — and what she represents as the thing Victorian England locked away rather than accommodate.

angleCards.title: Rochester as romantic hero — or not.
angleCards.text: Rochester is compelling, but he deceives Jane, keeps a wife locked away, and nearly commits bigamy. I want to track whether the novel ultimately rewards him or holds him accountable.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Jane Eyre to assess Rochester — to understand whether he's a romantic hero who deserves redemption or a man who needed a serious lesson, and whether the novel's ending vindicates or punishes him.

angleCards.title: Jane's navigation of religion.
angleCards.text: Three kinds of religious authority compete for Jane — cold institutional piety, warm self-sacrifice, and burning zealotry. I want to understand what Brontë is arguing through each of them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Jane Eyre to follow how Jane navigates religion — from the cold institutional piety of Brocklehurst to the warmth of Helen Burns to the dangerous zealotry of St. John Rivers.

cast.name: Jane Eyre
cast.description: Plain, poor, and absolutely certain of her own value. She tells her own story in her own voice — one of the most distinctive first-person narrators in English fiction. She is almost always right.

cast.name: Mr. Rochester
cast.description: Dark, restless, and in possession of a secret that will change everything. He falls in love with Jane partly because she refuses to flatter him. The most complicated love interest in Victorian fiction.

cast.name: Bertha Mason
cast.description: Rochester's first wife, kept on the third floor of Thornfield. The source of the novel's Gothic atmosphere and its deepest moral problem. She is never given her own voice.

cast.name: St. John Rivers
cast.description: A beautiful, cold, supremely ambitious missionary who wants Jane as an instrument of God's work. The novel's most frightening suitor — because his demands come wrapped in righteousness.

cast.name: Helen Burns
cast.description: Jane's only friend at Lowood school. Stoic, principled, and shortly dying. She teaches Jane to endure what cannot be changed — and then dies, leaving Jane to apply the lesson alone.

cast.name: Mrs. Reed
cast.description: Jane's aunt, who raises her with contempt and excludes her from the family. The original injustice that shapes everything. Jane confronts her twice — and the second confrontation is one of the novel's great scenes.

whyItMatters.title: A Voice That Insists on Itself
whyItMatters.body: Jane is poor, plain, and small — and the novel is built around her insistence that she is the moral equal of anyone she meets. The voice is the argument. Reading it now you can still feel why this kind of first-person was startling in 1847.

whyItMatters.title: The Madwoman in the Attic
whyItMatters.body: The discovery of Bertha — Rochester's first wife, kept in the attic of Thornfield — is one of the most discussed reveals in Victorian fiction. Critics have read it as everything from gothic plot device to repressed double of Jane herself. The novel will not let either reading be simple.

whyItMatters.title: Marriage on Equal Terms
whyItMatters.body: The novel's conclusion is unusual for its era: Jane will marry Rochester only when she is independently wealthy and he has been physically diminished. The argument about what a real partnership requires is direct and uncompromising.
